about.title: El Cerrito Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Falls happen fast, but proving a premises liability claim in El Cerrito takes patience and evidence. Under California law, a property owner isn't automatically responsible just because someone got hurt on their floor or sidewalk — you generally have to show they knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn you. That could be a wet floor near an entrance on San Pablo Avenue, a cracked walkway outside a shop off Potrero Avenue, or poor lighting in a stairwell. Because stores and property managers often erase surveillance footage within days or weeks, getting the incident documented quickly matters. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we're a free service that connects injured El Cerrito residents with independent attorneys who understand how to investigate notice, preserve video, and evaluate what a fall claim may be worth given California's comparative fault rules.

items.title: We understand the notice requirement
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. Attorneys in our network know how to dig into maintenance logs, inspection records, and prior complaints to build that case.

items.title: Surveillance video disappears fast
items.desc: Many El Cerrito businesses overwrite security footage within days. An attorney can send a preservation letter quickly, before evidence of the hazard is gone for good.

items.title: Comparative fault won't automatically sink your claim
items.desc: Even if you were partly distracted or moving quickly when you fell, California's pure comparative fault rule means you may still recover a share of damages reduced by your percentage of fault.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in El Cerrito?
items.answer: Generally you have two years from the date of the fall under California law. If the property involved is owned by a government entity — such as a city sidewalk near San Pablo Avenue or a BART-adjacent lot — the deadline to file a claim is much shorter, sometimes just six months. It's worth having this reviewed early so you don't lose your options.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for my own fall?
items.answer: California follows pure comparative fault, so being partially responsible doesn't bar you from recovery. Your compensation would simply be reduced by your percentage of fault. An attorney can help assess how fault might be allocated in your specific situation.

items.question: What should I do right after a fall in a store or parking lot?
items.answer: If you're able, take photos of the hazard, note the time and location, and ask if a manager can preserve any surveillance footage. Reporting the incident and seeking medical evaluation soon after also helps document what happened, which can matter later if you connect with an attorney.
